title: The Front Porch and the Black Bag: Warren G. Harding, Normalcy, and Teapot Dome
subtitle: Behind the punchline of America's 'worst president'—a small-town editor who forged the federal budget and disarmed battleships while old poker friends looted the vault
location: Marion Front Porch, Washington Naval Hall, Teapot Dome Flats & Palace Hotel, San Francisco
epigraph: “I have no trouble with my enemies. I can take care of my enemies all right. But my damn friends, my god-damned friends, White, they're the ones who keep me walking the floor nights!” — Warren G. Harding, conversation with William Allen White, 1923
keyContext: Exhausted by European trenches, pandemic flu, and bitter treaty deadlock, millions of voters in 1920 longed for a calm small-town executive who wouldn't lecture them from a pedestal. Out of central Ohio stepped a silver-haired newspaper publisher promising steady paychecks and ordinary sense, propelled toward Chicago's convention hall by tough political operators working behind closed doors. Could an amiable editor steady a shaken Washington—or would personal loyalty turn dangerous once old friends carried keys to federal offices?
paragraphs: Fresh gravel crunched under heavy wingtip shoes along Mount Vernon Avenue in Marion, Ohio, as visiting delegations filed across Warren Harding's front lawn during the summer of 1920. Standing atop painted porch steps in crisp cream linen, the silver-haired senator shook every hand in reach and pitched warm phrases in a resonant Chautauqua baritone. Beside him, his sharp-eyed wife Florence—nicknamed the Duchess by local reporters—waved newsreel crews into line and kept iced lemonade pitchers moving. Whenever cameras clicked, Harding leaned down with effortless small-town grace. By dusk, trainloads of farmers and shopkeepers rode home convinced they'd met an honest neighbor fit for the White House.

That front porch wasn't stagecraft; it was the only world Harding truly mastered. At age nineteen in 1884, he scraped together three hundred dollars with two partners to buy a struggling sheet called the Marion Star. On its newsroom wall he posted a printed reporter creed demanding decency and factual accuracy. Florence stepped behind the ledger desk, chasing delinquent ad bills and drilling paperboys until their daily ruled central Ohio. Elected to the Senate in 1915, Harding barely rocked the boat while post-war inflation exhausted voters. Addressing Boston merchants on May 14, 1920, he declared America needed healing over heroics and normalcy over nostrums.

Weeks later in June, Chicago's Republican convention deadlocked between competing generals and governors until power brokers gathered at two in the morning inside Room 404 of the Blackstone Hotel. Political manager Harry Daugherty had famously predicted fifteen bleary-eyed men in a smoke-filled room would settle on his amiable Ohio senator. He got his wish before sunrise. Party leaders picked Harding partly because he offended nobody—though panic struck once his longtime Marion mistress Carrie Fulton Phillips threatened to release passionate war-era love letters. Republican managers discreetly handed her family twenty-five thousand dollars and booked them onto a slow Pacific voyage to Japan until November's sixty-percent landslide closed.
Small-town geniality sold papers and carried states. Inside executive suites, that same reluctance to tell an old friend no proved lethal.

Taking office during a sharp 1921 depression that left five million workers—roughly twelve percent of the labor force—without paychecks, Harding backed serious cabinet talent. He tapped Charles Evans Hughes at State, Andrew Mellon at Treasury, and Herbert Hoover at Commerce. Working with that economic team, Harding convened a September 1921 unemployment conference urging mayors to speed local public works. Mellon simultaneously pushed the Revenue Act of 1921, dropping peak individual income surtaxes from seventy-three percent down to fifty-eight. Harding also shattered his predecessor's icy wartime silence toward the press. He welcomed White House reporters twice weekly for live questions, openly admitting when complex tax details stumped him.

Next, Harding's team fixed a glaring fiscal blind spot inside federal spending. Before 1921, executive agencies sent separate wish lists directly to scattered congressional subcommittees without one coordinated ledger. Nobody knew annual outlays until bills arrived. Signing the Budget and Accounting Act on June 10, 1921, Harding required one consolidated presidential spending plan each year and launched the Bureau of the Budget beside an independent General Accounting Office. First director Charles Dawes marched before federal purchasing chiefs waving two ordinary sweeping tools. He exposed three hundred fifty thousand surplus Army twine brooms sitting idle while the Navy bought wire-bound handles at retail down the block, slashing government waste within a single year.

Autumn brought diplomatic fireworks to Washington. On November 12, 1921—one day after dedicating Arlington's Tomb of the Unknown Soldier—envoys from nine maritime powers filled Washington's white-pillared Memorial Continental Hall. A single new dreadnought cost roughly forty million dollars, threatening bankruptcy from London to Tokyo. Following Harding's warm welcome, Secretary of State Hughes dropped diplomatic pleasantries for thirty-five electrifying minutes. He read aloud the names of sixty-six American, British, and Japanese warships and proposed scrapping them all immediately. Stunned London correspondents wrote that Hughes had sunk more capital hulls in half an hour than every admiral in centuries. On February 6, 1922, diplomats signed the Five-Power Treaty capping capital fleets at 525,000 tons apiece for Britain and America, 315,000 for Japan, and 175,000 each for France and Italy. Paired Four-Power and Nine-Power pacts dissolved the tense Anglo-Japanese Alliance and pressured Tokyo to return China's Shandong Peninsula.

Harding startled critics on race and civil liberties too. On October 26, 1921, he traveled deep into Jim Crow Alabama to mark Birmingham's fiftieth birthday before a massive crowd divided by heavy rope barriers in Woodrow Wilson Park. Facing stony white grandstands and cheering Black bleachers, Harding condemned lynching as barbarism. Whether listeners liked it or not, he declared, democracy stood exposed as a lie unless Black citizens gained equal political and economic rights. He backed Missouri Representative Leonidas Dyer's federal anti-lynching bill through the House in 1922 before Southern Senate filibusters strangled it. On December 23, 1921, Harding also commuted Socialist leader Eugene Debs's ten-year Espionage sentence and freed twenty-three other wartime prisoners. Greeting the old agitator at the White House the morning after Christmas, Harding grinned and said he'd heard so damned much about him he was glad to meet him personally.
Daylight saw cabinet reforms advance smoothly. Nighttime upstairs told a far murkier story.

After hours inside his second-floor White House study, Harding shed formal stiffness for cigar smoke and bootleg bourbon over high-stakes poker with cronies dubbed the Ohio Gang. Men who'd cheered his Senate climb now carried federal keys inside their coat pockets. Harding hated refusing favors or suspecting friends of theft. That blind spot proved ruinous across three separate offices.

The boldest plunder started under routine paperwork barely three months into Harding's presidency. Years earlier, Presidents Taft and Wilson had locked oil-rich tracts at Wyoming's sandstone-rimmed Teapot Dome and California's Elk Hills inside Navy vaults to guarantee emergency warship fuel. Interior Secretary Albert Fall, a debt-ridden former New Mexico senator, claimed adjacent private drillers were siphoning oil sideways out of federal pools—a technical excuse called drainage. Persuading pliable Navy Secretary Edwin Denby and Harding to sign Executive Order 3474 on May 31, 1921, Fall shifted those fields under Interior control. By April 1922, the secretary skipped competitive bidding altogether, leasing Teapot Dome to Harry Sinclair's Mammoth Oil Company and handing Elk Hills to Edward Doheny's Pan-American Petroleum. Months earlier, the California oilman's son had carried a little black satchel holding one hundred thousand dollars cash straight to Fall as an unrecorded loan. Soon afterward, Sinclair sweetened the secretary's New Mexico ranch with roughly three hundred thousand dollars in Liberty bonds and prized livestock.

Across town at the newly built Veterans' Bureau, Harding's jovial wartime acquaintance Charles Forbes turned wounded soldiers' care into open theft. Working through Boston salvage dealers Thompson and Kelly out of Maryland's Perryville supply depot, Forbes unloaded carloads of spotless sheets and surgical gauze at fractions of cost. He pocketed steady kickbacks on hospital construction sites too. Over two hundred million public dollars vanished or went to waste. Early in 1923, White House physician Charles Sawyer exposed the Perryville invoices and tipped off Harding. An eyewitness watched the normally mild president pin Forbes against a study wall by his throat and curse him for a double-crossing traitor. Yet Harding dreaded public scandal and let Forbes resign to sail for Europe rather than call prosecutors.

Down at 1625 K Street, Attorney General Harry Daugherty's closest confidant Jesse Smith ran an open backdoor marketplace. Fixers peddled Prohibition withdrawal permits freeing bonded whiskey from federal warehouses alongside pardons and seized German corporate assets. By May 1923, rumors burned too hot to contain. Weeks after Harding ordered him barred from White House grounds, the Ohio fixer fired a revolver inside Daugherty's Wardman Park apartment on May 30 and died.

Shaken by Smith's gunshot and plagued by spiking blood pressure, Harding packed trunks in June for a cross-country Voyage of Understanding meant to rally voters ahead of 1924. Crossing Kansas wheat fields and Colorado passes, he boarded the Navy transport Henderson in Tacoma to become the first sitting president in Alaska Territory. Aboard ship, coded Washington dispatches unsettled his staff. Chest pains flared during evening card games. At Nenana he hammered a golden spike along the Alaska Railroad, forcing smiles through dockside parades as Secretary Herbert Hoover watched a haunted chief privately ask what a man did when friends betrayed him. Speaking under blistering July sun in Seattle, Harding stumbled badly over typed pages before doctors canceled Portland and rushed his special train south toward San Francisco.

Physicians carried Harding into eighth-floor Suite 8064 at the Palace Hotel, where fever and breathless exhaustion pinned him against the pillows. White House homeopath Sawyer blamed tainted Alaskan crab meat and promised rapid recovery. Navy doctor Joel Boone and Stanford's Ray Lyman Wilbur pressed stethoscopes against an enlarged, failing heart. On August 2, 1923, Harding propped himself up briefly while Florence read aloud Samuel Blythe's glowing Saturday Evening Post profile titled A Calm Review of a Calm Man. That's good, go on, Harding whispered at 7:35 p.m., right before shuddering once. Moments later, his heart stopped. Florence barred an autopsy, rode the mourning train eastward, and spent days in Marion feeding his private papers into a hearth.

Smoke from that Ohio fireplace couldn't erase contracts locked inside Washington filing cabinets. Trouble had already sparked back in April 1922, when Wyoming oilmen spotted Mammoth Oil trucks rolling onto Teapot Dome without public bidding and alerted Wyoming Senator John Kendrick. Days later a Wall Street Journal scoop exposed Fall's closed-door deals, forcing Senate Republican chiefs to launch an inquiry under junior Montana Democrat Thomas Walsh—expecting the modest Western lawyer to find nothing. Instead, Walsh spent eighteen grinding months reading dusty land registries and tracing bank envelopes until a Denver witness shattered Doheny's cash-loan cover story and exposed Sinclair's hidden bonds.

Four years after Harding's death, the Supreme Court voided those fraudulent oil leases in 1927, and Albert Fall entered a New Mexico cell in 1931 as the first Cabinet officer imprisoned for crimes in office. Charles Forbes served time at Leavenworth penitentiary, while Harry Daugherty walked free after two hung juries. Inside Treasury and Budget Bureau offices, clerks continued running the unified annual ledgers Harding's team had built in 1921. Across town, Senate archivists locked away boxes of oil subpoenas while soot cooled inside Marion's hearth.

analysis.heading: 1. The Unresolved Debate
analysis.paragraph: For four decades after his death, historians mocked Harding as an amiable cipher wholly blind to governance. Archival researcher Robert Murray overturned that caricature in 1969 with The Harding Era. His work showed Harding's cabinet lifted America swiftly out of the 1921 depression, slicing annual federal outlays from over five billion dollars to roughly three point three billion while building lasting fiscal tools. Later biographers Eugene Trani and David Wilson struck a sharper balance. They credit Harding with authentic courage on naval arms limits and Southern racial violence while arguing his deep terror of personal conflict crippled oversight long before Teapot Dome broke. Scholars still disagree over whether he stayed willfully blind or overwhelmed by Washington.

analysis.heading: 2. The Road Not Taken
analysis.paragraph: Had Harding's heart held out past August 1923, Senator Thomas Walsh's explosive oil hearings would've landed squarely on the president's own desk. Instead of his quiet New England successor scrubbing the party clean behind terse silence, an aging Harding must've faced the storm himself. That fight couldn't have stayed polite for long. Either he'd have fired Attorney General Daugherty publicly to salvage a 1924 re-election bid, or House Democrats were poised to launch the first presidential impeachment crisis since Andrew Johnson. Either outcome might've fractured Republican dominance in the Roaring Twenties years before the 1929 crash and altered national politics early.

analysis.heading: 3. How It Shapes Daily Life Today
analysis.paragraph: Every February, when the White House transmits one consolidated federal budget binder to Capitol Hill, Washington runs on Harding's 1921 machinery. Both the modern Office of Management and Budget and Congress's nonpartisan Government Accountability Office descend straight from that June statute, guiding federal audits every single quarter. Congressional subpoena power carries an equally direct lineage. When Daugherty's brother defied Senate investigators probing Justice Department graft, the Supreme Court ruled in 1927's McGrain versus Daugherty that lawmakers hold constitutional authority to compel witness testimony and seize financial records. That precedent anchors every televised congressional oversight hearing across Capitol Hill today.

analysis.heading: 4. Essential Books, Films & Places to Go Deeper
analysis.paragraph: Start with former White House counsel John Dean's crisp biography Warren G. Harding for an insider's eye on how personal loyalty turns into cover-up. Follow it with Laton McCartney's gripping chronicle The Teapot Dome Scandal and Phillip Payne's cultural history Dead Last, tracing how gossip reshaped presidential memory for decades. Readers curious about Harding's private life can also examine Nan Britton's 1927 memoir The President's Daughter alongside 2015 genetic testing confirming paternity. That front porch in Marion looks remarkably modest today. Tour the restored Harding Home and Presidential Library in Marion, Ohio, or walk through San Francisco's historic Palace Hotel to trace his final western corridor.
